scenes.vo: October twenty-eighteen. India's Supreme Court bans crackers made with barium salts, and joined crackers.
In Sivakasi, the town that makes most of India's fireworks, the factories go quiet. For about five months.
How does a town get this big, and this exposed to a single rule? The road starts a hundred years earlier, with a matchbox.
Follow the road. Try, but, so.
Find India on the globe. Now slide down to its far south, to Tamil Nadu.
Sivakasi sits in Virudhunagar district. It is hot, and it sits in the rain shadow of the hills to the west.
Farming here is hard, and families nearby need work. Villages around Sivakasi have plenty of labour, and little to do with it.
Three things to keep in mind. A match. A Bengal light, which is a match that burns in colour. And a firework.
Go back to nineteen twenty-two. Matches are made in Calcutta, today's Kolkata, or shipped in from abroad.
Two young men from Sivakasi make that trip. P. Ayya Nadar is about seventeen. A. Shanmuga Nadar is about nineteen.
They aren't going to learn fireworks. They're going to learn one thing: how to make a safety match.
They stay six to eight months, learning from a match-maker named Purna Chandra Roy.
In nineteen twenty-three they come home with German machines and open a match factory. The South-India Lucifer Match Industry.
But the German machines are costly to run in a small, remote town.
So they change the plan. They spread the work across the villages, to families with time to spare.
Families roll, fill and pack by hand, at home. The factory does only the chemical part.
It fits the mood of the time. Mahatma Gandhi is urging Indians to revive village industries.
Remember that choice. It builds the town. And a hundred years later, it is the hardest thing to change.
In nineteen twenty-six the two men part ways, and compete. Ayya Nadar's brand is a squirrel, Anil. Shanmuga Nadar's is a crow, Kaaka. A squirrel against a crow.
But a plain wooden match doesn't stand out. And each of the two rivals wants to.
To stand out, match-makers add something new: sticks that burn in colour. They're called Bengal lights. In Tamil, matthaappu.

Local histories treat the Bengal light as the stepping stone. A match that burns in colour is already close to a sparkler. And in nineteen thirty-eight, N. R. K. Rajarathina Nadar opens the town's first factory made only for fireworks.
So matches led to coloured matches, and coloured matches led to fireworks. Not a tradition. A chain.
So far: a match, a hand network, a coloured flame. Each fixed the last problem.
Every matchbox and every packet of crackers needs a bright paper label. In the nineteen thirties, those labels come from presses in Bombay, today's Mumbai.
But waiting for labels from Bombay is slow. So in nineteen thirty-eight, K. S. A. Arunagiri Nadar sets up a printing press in Sivakasi itself.

Picture a shop that sells most of its stock in one week, and keeps running out of paper cups from a far-off city. So the owner buys a printer. Then he notices it can print for the other eleven months too.
That is Sivakasi's second trick. When the fireworks season ends, the presses keep running. Calendars. Diaries. Notebooks.
Prime Minister Nehru is said to have called the town 'Kutty Japan', Little Japan, for making matches, fireworks and print on its own.
A historian of the town, Rengaiah Murugan, put it simply: 'As a chain reaction, various allied industries started to mushroom.'
So three links so far. The match. The coloured flame. The press. One more is coming, and it is not a machine. It is a war.
Now comes the moment that turns a good town into the national one. Nineteen-forty.
That year, the Explosives Rules arrive. To make fireworks, you now need a licence.
Then the Second World War cuts off the fireworks that used to come in from abroad.
The few licensed makers suddenly have the whole market. By nineteen forty-two, three firms hold licences: National, Standard and Kaliswari.
Three licensed factories in nineteen forty-two.
By nineteen eighty: a hundred and eighty-nine.
By two thousand and one: four hundred and fifty.
Today, the industry says, more than a thousand.
Worth about six thousand crore rupees a year. That is sixty billion rupees.
Notice the pattern. Every step solved the last problem, and set up the next one.
That is the road up. Now back to the quiet sheds of twenty-eighteen.
But the ban hits barium, a core ingredient of the old recipe. For about five months, the town waits.
The industry's answer is the green cracker, developed by a government lab, CSIR-NEERI. Its versions are called SWAS, SAFAL and STAR.
Green doesn't mean pollution-free. The lab's own claim is about a third less particle pollution.
How? According to the lab, the mix releases water vapour and air as it burns, which helps the dust settle. Picture a tiny mist sprayer inside the shell.
Delhi and its surroundings are roughly thirteen percent of national demand, industry associations estimate.

But even the fix has a catch. In October twenty twenty-five, the Court eases the Delhi ban for green crackers only, with QR codes, in fixed time slots. It comes just before Deepavali. A makers' leader said it comes too close to the festival, yet gives hope for future business.
So the fix is real, and it is partial. Less pollution, not none. And a market that opens in slots.
Now go back to the hands. By the industry's count, about three lakh people work in these factories. That is three hundred thousand. Many more work around them.
Mixing, filling and threading fuses are still done mostly by hand.
On paper, a small unit's licence limits how many people may work inside. Reports say twelve.
Reports describe sheds sub-let to contractors, and crowded verandahs. A gap between the licence and the workplace.
On the nineteenth of April, twenty twenty-six, an explosion at a factory near Sivakasi killed twenty-five workers.
A worker, K. Rajkumar, told The Hindu that with a biometric attendance system, identifying the dead would not have been so hard.
The road began with a choice to spread the work across many hands. It built the town. Now the same choice asks for a new safety answer.
In May twenty twenty-five, the makers' association applied for a GI tag for Sivakasi fireworks. It's a legal label of origin. Their lawyer says it would help curb duplicates.
Try, but, so. A match, then hands. A flame, then a press. A war, then a market. A ban, then a green recipe.
In twenty-eighteen the lights went out in Sivakasi. The town did not make fireworks for centuries. It learned to make them, one fix at a time.
Its next fix is the hardest: to keep the people who light the sky safe.
